episodes.title: David Ayliffe: 23 Years in a Cult, an ADHD Late Diagnosis at 70, and the Day the Film Over His Eyes Fell Away
episodes.description: The film over the eyes fell away ⚠️ Content advisory: this episode discusses mental health & wellbeing, which some listeners may find distressing. If you need support, you're not alone. Help is available: • Lifeline (24/7 crisis support): 13 11 14 · lifeline.org.au David's career began in journalism at the Bankstown Observer, where he worked alongside young Paul Keating. His ADHD, undiagnosed until age 70, drove him through multiple careers and into a Pentecostal healing ministry that became a cult led by a woman claiming to be God. For 23 years, he was isolated from family, including hanging up on his mother's calls. After the cult leader died, David led a five-year dismantling process, reversing isolation, reconnecting members with families, and eventually dissolving the group. He has since worked for International Needs, the Red Cross, Guide Dogs Victoria, and now runs a disability support business. His vision centres on kindness as a practice and framework for society, taught through children. David Ayliffe is a journalist, charity CEO, disability support worker and children's book author who spent 23 years in a religious cult before dismantling it from within. Now 72 and recently diagnosed with ADHD, he works with people with intellectual disabilities and advocates for kindness as a foundation for society. In this Kintsugi Heroes conversation with John Milham, David shares the story behind the moments below. 🎙️ IN THIS CONVERSATION: • Late ADHD diagnosis can reframe decades of 'failures' and offer self-compassion instead of shame. • Fundamentalism thrives by declaring certainty; it requires turning off critical thinking by designating something sacred. • Cult recovery works when the leader loses credibility; collective realization can dismantle even deep isolation in a single moment. 🕒 CHAPTERS: 00:00 Young David at the Bankstown Observer 06:17 ADHD diagnosis at 70 16:19 The path into the cult: from journalist to believer 22:09 How fundamentalism silences critical thinking 27:20 Cut off from everyone but her 32:35 The moment she lost all credibility 35:28 The Emperor's New Clothes moment 37:48 The dismantling: five years of reversal and reconnection 42:04 Disability work and the kindness vision 51:00 Kindness as something you practise 56:51 Admitting what you got wrong 1:03:17 Humour as the thing that saved me 🎧 If this story moved you, follow Kintsugi Heroes in your podcast app so you never miss an episode. 📌 RESOURCES MENTIONED: Lifeline Australia: lifeline.org.au ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ ABOUT KINTSUGI HEROES ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ Welcome. episodes.title: Leaving A Cult At 18: How Queer Support Services Saved My Life
episodes.description:
Growing up in a controlling religious cult, our hero was told who to be and how to feel. At 18, after their family's reaction to their non-binary identity escalated from verbal abuse to physical threats, they left home with almost nothing. In this episode of Pride in Stories, they share the concrete steps that kept them safe: contacting queer support services, planning before leaving, asking friends clearly for help, navigating Centrelink, and legally changing their name. Today they're thriving at university, surrounded by chosen family, and researching gender-affirming care for non-binary people. A raw story about family violence prevention, chosen identity, and what it takes to rebuild.

At our hero's request, we've withheld their name and identifying details to protect their privacy.

⚠️ Content advisory: this episode discusses abuse & exploitation and domestic & family violence, which some listeners may find distressing.

If you need support, you're not alone — help is available:
• Blue Knot Foundation (complex trauma): 1300 657 380 · blueknot.org.au
• 1800RESPECT (family, domestic & sexual violence): 1800 737 732 · 1800respect.org.au

Family violence is not always visible. For our hero, it began as control and suppression in a closed religious environment, escalated to verbal and emotional abuse when they came out as non-binary, and turned to physical threats when they refused to hide. Yet the turning point-the gold in the cracks-came from a network of people and services most young people don't know exist.

This episode maps the concrete steps our hero took: contacting Pride in Place and Rainbow Door before leaving home, creating a safety plan, obtaining a new phone number their family couldn't track, couch-surfing with supportive friends, accessing Centrelink within the critical seven-day window, and legally changing their name (easier and cheaper than expected). It's a masterclass in planning for safety, not a tragedy narrative.

But the story doesn't end there.

🕒 CHAPTERS:
00:00 Growing up in a controlling religious home
04:45 A waistcoat and a cousin's fear
09:51 The day I decided to leave
11:46 Disconnecting: a new phone, a new identity
15:34 Safety took months, not days
18:14 The friends who showed up
23:31 Refusing to die as the wrong person
25:25 The everyday miracles: friends over, plans made
32:43 Research for non-binary gender-affirming care
36:04 Verbal abuse counts as abuse
37:15 Five years on, still building
39:39 What comes next
